I've drafted the section below. One thing to know first: I don't know your study's design or argument, so the draft surveys the whole field and ends with a placeholder where you say how your paper fits in. It's organized around the main explanations researchers give for why trust goes one way or the other. I read the abstracts of the papers I describe in detail. A few others are cited on their titles or short summaries only, and I list those at the end.

---

## Related Work

### Algorithms usually outperform people, yet people often resist them

The puzzle goes back to the "clinical versus actuarial" debate in psychology: is human judgment or a formula better at prediction? Statistical rules, even crude ones, tend to match or beat expert judgment [W2056418346; W2102256472]. A meta-analysis of studies on human health and behavior found mechanical prediction about 10% more accurate on average. Experts were substantially more accurate in only 6–16% of studies, and this held across tasks, types of judges and levels of experience [W2168729696]. If people judged advice only by its accuracy, they would favor algorithms. Much of the research since asks why they often don't, and why they sometimes do.

### Algorithm aversion

Dietvorst, Simmons and Massey named the effect *algorithm aversion*. In five incentivized studies, people who watched an algorithm make forecasts lost confidence in it and chose an inferior human forecaster instead, even when they had seen the algorithm do better. People lost confidence in an algorithm faster than in a human after seeing both make the same mistake [W3125633690]. Prahl and Van Swol did not find a general preference for human advisors. They did find that use of automated advice dropped more sharply than use of human advice after bad advice, and that people felt they had more in common with human advisors [W2600700815]. So the clearest form of aversion is an unforgiving reaction to algorithm errors, not a blanket preference for humans.

Aversion is also reported where algorithms clearly win. Yeomans et al. found that recommender systems predicted which jokes people would find funny better than strangers, friends or family did. People still preferred human recommenders, partly because they found the human process easier to understand [W2913854599]. In healthcare, Longoni, Bonezzi and Morewedge found that consumers were less willing to use AI providers, would pay less for them, and were less sensitive to differences in how well providers performed. The driver was "uniqueness neglect": the belief that AI cannot account for a person's individual circumstances [W2942858056]. Dietvorst and Bharti suggest a decision-theoretic explanation. People are less and less bothered by each extra unit of forecasting error, so in unpredictable domains they prefer riskier, higher-variance methods such as human judgment, which seem more likely to produce a near-perfect answer [W2974452734].

### Algorithm appreciation

Other studies find the opposite. In six experiments, Logg, Minson and Moore found that lay people followed advice more when they thought it came from an algorithm than from a person, an effect they called *algorithm appreciation*. It held across visual estimates and forecasts of song popularity and romantic attraction, and researchers had predicted the reverse. The effect weakened when people compared the algorithm with their own judgment rather than another advisor's, and among experienced forecasters, who relied on it less and lost accuracy as a result [W2800068874]. Later studies support appreciation in judge–advisor tasks. You, Yang and Li found it held even when the algorithm's prediction errors were disclosed in summary form, but declined when performance information was presented in a more detailed, cognitively demanding format [W4281822284]. Bogert, Schecter and Watson found people relied more on algorithmic advice than on a crowd of peers as tasks got harder, while still penalizing wrong advice more when it was labelled as algorithmic [W3152500611].

Appreciation can turn into over-reliance. Banker and Khetani showed that consumers followed algorithmic recommendations even when they were worse, because they believed algorithms had more domain expertise [W4248125493]. In the public sector, Alon-Barkat and Busuioc found no automation bias (algorithmic advice was not followed more than equivalent expert advice). They did find "selective adherence", meaning advice was followed more when it matched stereotypes, regardless of whether it came from an algorithm or a human expert [W4211002924]. Chong et al. found that people's confidence in themselves, more than their confidence in the AI, drove whether they accepted AI suggestions. People sometimes blamed themselves for errors and kept relying on a poorly performing AI [W3199747482]. Together these studies suggest the real question is whether reliance is appropriate, not simply whether there is more or less of it. Human-factors research on trust in automation has long made this point [W4243342770].

### Reconciling the two

Several reviews have tried to explain the mixed findings. Burton, Stein and Jensen reviewed 61 articles and grouped the causes of aversion into five themes: expectations and expertise, decision autonomy, incentives, cognitive compatibility, and differing rationalities [W2981686111]. Jussupow, Benbasat and Heinzl synthesized 84 experimental studies and pointed to the algorithm's agency, performance, perceived capabilities and level of human involvement, along with the user's expertise and social distance [W3024435124]. Mahmud et al. reviewed the same literature [W4200546216]. Glikson and Woolley's review of trust in AI highlights tangibility, transparency, reliability and immediacy as drivers of cognitive trust, and anthropomorphism as a driver of emotional trust [W3013998503].

Some work argues the split is partly a matter of study design. Hou and Jung produced both aversion and appreciation by changing only how the human and algorithmic advisors were described, with perceived competence (expert power) explaining the difference [W3206874785]. Jussupow et al. later showed that studies differ in what they compare: an algorithm against a human advisor, against one's own judgment, or against combinations. They argue the expected direction of preference depends on this setup [W4400803056]. This fits Logg et al.'s finding that appreciation weakens when the algorithm competes with the self [W2800068874].

Below we group the main explanations into four clusters.

**(a) Task and domain.** Lee found algorithmic managerial decisions were seen as just as fair and trustworthy as human ones for "mechanical" tasks. For tasks seen as requiring human skills they were seen as less fair and trustworthy, because algorithms were thought to lack intuition and subjective judgment [W2792183666]. People also resist machines making moral decisions, partly because machines are seen as unable to fully think or feel [W2886363025]. They object to algorithms making morally relevant tradeoffs because algorithms are assumed to maximize outcomes [W3181173654]. Higher task difficulty or complexity, in contrast, tends to increase reliance on algorithms [W3152500611; W3193926864].

**(b) Beliefs about what algorithms can do.** Common lay beliefs drive aversion: that algorithms ignore individual uniqueness [W2942858056], cannot learn from mistakes [W4283162852], or are harder to understand [W2913854599]. Beliefs that AI is smarter than humans drive appreciation [W3193926864; W4248125493]. Showing that an algorithm can learn reduces aversion [W3110817755; W4283162852]. Turel and Kalhan add an implicit, unconscious prejudice against AI that shapes early reliance and fades as people get diagnostic information about how the AI performs [W4391114267].

**(c) Control and transparency.** Letting people modify an algorithm's forecasts even slightly greatly increases its use [W3121705224]. A replication partly confirmed this effect, raised reproducibility concerns, and found that some forms of control over the algorithm's design, such as choosing the training algorithm, also help [W4366547314]. Transparency does not always help: revealing an algorithm that seems too simple reduces use of its advice, while revealing one that seems too complex has no significant effect [W3189444386].

**(d) Errors and how trust changes over time.** Seeing algorithms err is the most consistent trigger of aversion [W3125633690; W2600700815; W3152500611]. Familiarity with an advisor matters too: Berger et al. found no difference in reliance on unfamiliar human and algorithmic advisors, but did find differences once people had seen familiar advisors err, and showing that the algorithm could learn removed the gap [W3110817755]. These results connect to the trust-in-automation tradition, where trust is a dynamic quantity adjusted through experience [W4243342770].

### Positioning

Overall, attitudes toward algorithms are neither uniformly negative nor uniformly positive. They depend on the task, what is being compared, how the algorithm is framed, beliefs about its capabilities, and the history of its performance. *[Add 2–3 sentences on how your paper fits in, e.g., whether it tests a reconciling mechanism, studies appropriate rather than total reliance, or looks at a new domain or moderator.]*

{"id": "W1987352340", "doi": "10.1002/jclp.20180", "title": "The ethical implications of Paul Meehl's work on comparing clinical versus actuarial prediction methods", "abstract": "Paul E. Meehl's work comparing statistical versus actuarial prediction-and the large body of research that followed by others on the same topic-was mainly theoretical and empirical. Meehl also suggested that this work led to a \"practical\" conclusion, which was quite strong. The author argues that, in addition, it leads to an ethical conclusion, equally strong. Whether the scientific findings are combined with an overarching ethical principle that the best predictions possible should be made for clients, or whether these findings are framed as delineating what can be done for clients-and that clinicians ought not to attempt to do what they cannot-the conclusion is the same. Whenever statistical prediction rules (SPR's) are available for making a relevant prediction, they should be used in preference to intuition. ## Related Work

### Origins: the clinical–statistical debate

The question of when people should, and will, defer to formal procedures over human judgment started decades before the term "algorithm aversion" appeared. It began with what psychology called the clinical versus statistical (or actuarial) prediction debate. Meehl's 1954 book *Clinical versus Statistical Prediction* asked whether formalized mathematical rules or the clinician's judgment predicts patient outcomes better. Meehl was careful to note that the answer might vary by task [W2129871510]. Grove and Meehl later reviewed 136 studies covering many kinds of outcomes and concluded that the mechanical method "is almost invariably equal to or superior to" the clinical one. They also rebutted common anti-actuarial arguments and discussed why practitioners resist the evidence [W2102256472]. A meta-analysis of studies on human health and behavior agreed. Mechanical prediction was about 10% more accurate on average and substantially better in 33–47% of studies, while human judgment was substantially better in only 6–16%. This held regardless of task, type of judge or judges' experience [W2168729696].

Dawes went further. When a numerical outcome is predicted from numerical inputs, even "improper" linear models outperform clinical intuition, including models whose weights are set by intuition or simply set equal. Dawes also listed the technical, psychological and ethical objections people raise against using such models and offered counter-arguments [W2056418346]. Later he argued that when a validated statistical rule exists, using intuition instead is unethical [W1987352340].

So the field's founding observation already contained the paradox that drives current work: formal methods are usually more accurate, yet people resist them. Early studies of that resistance anticipated many later findings:

- **Experts believe their judgment is better.** In employee selection, Highhouse described two implicit beliefs: that near-perfect prediction is possible in principle, and that experience improves prediction of human behavior. Both lead people to rely too much on intuition and to avoid decision aids that might undermine their own credibility [W2171321543].
- **The public prefers clinical judgment.** In legal and medical scenarios, people rated clinical strategies above actuarial ones on preference, accuracy, fairness and ethics [W2150479185].
- **Using a computer aid lowers others' opinion of the user.** Patients rated physicians who used a computerized diagnostic aid less favorably than physicians who diagnosed unaided. Physicians who consulted a human colleague were not penalized in the same way, which suggests the penalty is about using a non-human tool, not about seeking advice in general [W2085105383].
- **People discount statistical advice when a human expert is the alternative.** In stock-price forecasting, Önkal et al. gave participants identical advice labelled as coming from either a human expert or a statistical method. Advice labelled statistical was discounted much more, and when both sources were offered side by side, people paid far more attention to the human expert [W2158570360].

The last study is the closest early version of the design we use: identical advice, with only the source label (algorithm or human expert) varied.

### Algorithm aversion

Dietvorst, Simmons and Massey gave the phenomenon its current name. In five incentivized forecasting studies, participants who had seen an algorithm perform were less confident in it and less likely to choose it over an inferior human forecaster, even when they had seen it outperform the human. The proposed mechanism is unequal forgiveness: people lose confidence in an algorithm faster than in a human after the same mistake [W3125633690]. Prahl and Van Swol did not replicate a general preference for human advisors. They did replicate the unequal response to errors, and found that people saw themselves as having more in common with human advisors [W2600700815].

Aversion is especially well documented in the taste-prediction tasks our study uses. Yeomans et al. found that recommender systems predicted which jokes people would find funny better than strangers, friends or even family. People still preferred human recommenders, partly because they found the human recommendation process easier to understand [W2913854599]. Earlier, on MovieLens, collaborative filtering outperformed human recommenders on average at predicting films a user would like, although some individuals beat the system substantially and humans did better on certain prediction tasks [W2075329139]. Taken together, these studies show a gap between actual and perceived accuracy that is largest in preference domains.

Other work identifies beliefs behind aversion. Consumers resist medical AI because of "uniqueness neglect", the concern that an algorithm cannot account for a person's individual characteristics [W2942858056]. They avoid algorithmic advice partly because they assume, often wrongly, that algorithms cannot learn from mistakes [W4283162852]. Dietvorst and Bharti offer a decision-theoretic account. People are less and less bothered by each additional unit of forecasting error, so in uncertain domains they prefer higher-variance methods such as human judgment, which seem more likely to give a near-perfect answer [W2974452734].

### Algorithm appreciation

The opposite effect is also well documented. In six experiments, Logg, Minson and Moore found that lay people followed advice more when they believed it came from an algorithm rather than a person, an effect they called *algorithm appreciation*. Notably, two of their tasks (forecasting song popularity and romantic attraction) are taste-related, close to the subjective end of our task range. Researchers had predicted the opposite result. Appreciation weakened when the algorithm was compared with participants' own judgment rather than an external advisor's, and among experienced forecasters, who relied less on algorithmic advice and became less accurate as a result [W2800068874].

Several later studies support appreciation in advice-taking paradigms:

- You, Yang and Li found people followed algorithmic advice more than identical human advice because they trusted the algorithm more. This held even when the algorithm's prediction errors were disclosed in summary form, but declined when performance information was presented in a more detailed, cognitively demanding format [W4281822284].
- Bogert, Schecter and Watson found people relied more on algorithmic advice than on a crowd of peers as tasks got harder. They still penalized inaccurate advice more when it was labelled algorithmic [W3152500611].
- Consumers who believe AI is smarter than humans are more likely to take algorithmic advice, but only when they see the task as complex [W3193926864].

Appreciation can also go too far. Banker and Khetani showed that consumers accepted inferior algorithmic recommendations because they believed algorithms had greater domain expertise [W4248125493]. Chong et al. found that people's self-confidence, more than their confidence in the AI, drove whether they accepted its suggestions, and that people sometimes blamed themselves and kept relying on a poorly performing AI [W3199747482]. These results support the human-factors view that the target is appropriate reliance, matched to how well the system actually performs, not reliance as such [W4243342770].

### Reconciling the findings: what moderates reliance

Reviews of this literature group the causes of aversion and appreciation into several themes [W2981686111; W3024435124; W4200546216]. Below we focus on the four most relevant to our design.

**Task objectivity and subjectivity.** The most consistent moderator is whether a task seems to call for measurable accuracy or for human sensibility. This idea goes back to Meehl's own caution that mechanical and clinical methods may suit different tasks [W2129871510].

- Lee found that for managerial decisions requiring "mechanical" skills, algorithmic and human decisions were seen as equally fair and trustworthy. For decisions requiring "human" skills, algorithmic decisions were judged less fair and trustworthy, because algorithms were seen as lacking intuition and subjective judgment [W2792183666].
- Jin and Li found that in less unstructured tasks, people trusted algorithms more than humans, explained by perceived accuracy. In highly unstructured tasks they trusted humans more, explained by perceived flexibility [W4415545653].
- Algorithmic work is seen as less authentic than human work in a moral (sincerity) sense, though not in terms of accuracy [W2754764889].
- People object to machines making moral decisions, partly because machines are seen as unable to fully think or feel [W2886363025]. They object to algorithms making morally relevant tradeoffs because algorithms are assumed to maximize outcomes [W3181173654].

The taste-prediction evidence, however, does not fit a simple objective/subjective split. Algorithms objectively win at predicting jokes and films [W2913854599; W2075329139], people avoid them for jokes [W2913854599], and yet people appreciate them for song and attraction forecasts [W2800068874]. This inconsistency suggests that perceived subjectivity, not the task itself, drives the effect. That is the gap our task range is designed to address.

**What the algorithm is compared with.** Whether people show aversion or appreciation depends on the alternative on offer. Logg et al. found appreciation when the comparison was another person, but it weakened when the comparison was the participant's own judgment [W2800068874]. Jussupow, Benbasat and Heinzl classify four decision setups (algorithm, human advisor, self, or combinations) and argue that the expected direction of preference differs across them [W4400803056]. The status of the human comparison also matters. Hou and Jung produced both aversion and appreciation by changing only how the human and algorithmic advisors were described, with perceived expertise explaining the difference [W3206874785]. Önkal et al. found the strongest discounting of statistical advice when it appeared next to a *human expert* [W2158570360]. Our algorithm-versus-expert choice therefore represents a demanding test for appreciation.

**Performance information and errors.** Seeing an algorithm err is the most reliable trigger of aversion [W3125633690; W2600700815; W3152500611]. Berger et al. found no difference in reliance on *unfamiliar* human and algorithmic advisors, but did find a difference once people had seen *familiar* advisors err, and showing that the algorithm could learn removed that gap [W3110817755]. Turel and Kalhan show that early reliance is shaped by implicit prejudice against AI, which fades as people receive diagnostic information about performance [W4391114267]. How performance information is presented also matters. Summary error information did not reduce appreciation, but more detailed information did [W4281822284]. Revealing how an algorithm works hurts reliance when the algorithm seems too simple, while seeming too complex has no significant effect [W3189444386].

**Control.** Letting people modify an algorithm's output, even slightly, greatly increases its use [W3121705224]. A replication partly confirmed this, raised reproducibility concerns, and found that letting users choose the training algorithm also helps [W4366547314].

### Summary and positioning

Seventy years after Meehl, the accuracy advantage of formal prediction is well established, but whether people act on it is not. Studies find aversion in some settings [W3125633690; W2913854599; W2158570360] and appreciation in others [W2800068874; W4281822284]. Task subjectivity and the type of comparison are the leading candidates for explaining the difference [W2792183666; W4400803056; W3206874785]. Read this way, the two findings need not conflict: aversion appears mainly after people see the algorithm err, and appreciation mainly when the algorithm is weighed against another advisor before any errors have been seen. The field's founding observation therefore already contained the paradox that drives current work: formal methods are usually more accurate, yet people resist them. Early studies of that resistance anticipated many later findings. In employee selection, Highhouse described two implicit beliefs that keep decision-makers relying on intuition: that near-perfect prediction is possible in principle, and that experience improves prediction of human behavior [W2171321543]. In legal and medical scenarios, people rated clinical strategies above actuarial ones on preference, accuracy, fairness and ethics [W2150479185].

The most direct early tests compared advice from a human expert with identical advice from a formal method. In stock-price forecasting, Önkal et al. found that advice labelled as coming from a statistical method was discounted much more than the same advice labelled as coming from a human expert, and that when both sources were offered together, people paid far more attention to the expert [W2158570360]. Promberger and Baron found the same pattern in medical decisions. Participants were more likely to follow a recommendation to have an operation when it came from a physician than when it came from a computer program, and they trusted the physician more to recommend well. The preference was partly explained by responsibility: following a physician's advice reduced participants' sense of personal responsibility more than following a computer's, and when advice came from the program, participants wanted to make the decision themselves more often [W2070125214]. Shaffer et al. found a related effect from the other side. Patients rated physicians who used a computerized diagnostic aid less favorably than physicians who diagnosed unaided, but did not penalize physicians who consulted a human colleague, suggesting the penalty is specific to relying on a non-human tool [W2085105383].

### Two landmark findings: algorithm aversion and algorithm appreciation

Two studies are now treated as the opposite ends of this debate. Dietvorst, Simmons and Massey gave the phenomenon its current name [W3125633690]. In five studies, participants saw forecasts from an algorithm, a human, both, or neither, and then decided whether to tie their incentives to the algorithm's or the human's future predictions. Participants who had seen the algorithm perform became less confident in it and less likely to choose it over an inferior human forecaster, even when they had seen it outperform the human. The authors trace this *algorithm aversion* to unequal forgiveness: people lose confidence in algorithmic forecasters faster than in human ones after seeing the same mistake.

Logg, Minson and Moore instead measured how much people adjusted their own estimates toward advice that was labelled as coming from an algorithm or from a person [W2800068874]. Across a series of experiments involving visual estimates and forecasts of song popularity and romantic attraction, lay participants adhered more to advice they believed came from an algorithm. This *algorithm appreciation* held whether advice was presented jointly or separately, and it ran against the predictions of a sample of researchers. It weakened in two conditions: when participants chose between the algorithm's estimate and their own rather than another advisor's, and among experienced forecasters, who relied less on algorithmic advice and lost accuracy as a result.

The studies differ in at least three respects. First, they measure different things: Dietvorst et al. measure a *choice* of which forecaster to rely on, while Logg et al. measure how much people *weight* advice. Second, they differ in exposure to performance. Aversion in Dietvorst et al. emerges after people see the algorithm perform and err, while Logg et al.'s appreciation is documented for advice received without that history. Third, they differ in the comparison: Logg et al. show that appreciation weakens when the alternative is one's own judgment rather than an external advisor.

Later work fits this reading. Prahl and Van Swol found no general preference for human advice but did replicate the steeper drop in reliance on automation after bad advice [W2600700815]. You, Yang and Li found that appreciation persisted when the algorithm's errors were disclosed in aggregate form but declined with more detailed performance information [W4281822284]. Jussupow, Benbasat and Heinzl argue that the expected direction of preference depends on whether the algorithm is compared with a human advisor, one's own judgment, or combinations of these [W4400803056]. Read this way, the two findings need not conflict: aversion appears mainly after people see the algorithm err, and appreciation mainly when the algorithm is weighed against another advisor before any errors have been seen.

### Further evidence for aversion

Aversion is especially well documented in the taste-prediction tasks our study uses. Yeomans et al. found that recommender systems predicted which jokes people would find funny better than strangers, friends or even family. People still preferred human recommenders, partly because they found the human recommendation process easier to understand [W2913854599]. Earlier, on MovieLens, collaborative filtering outperformed human recommenders on average at predicting films a user would like, although some individuals beat the system substantially and humans did better on certain prediction tasks [W2075329139]. Taken together, these studies show a gap between actual and perceived accuracy that is largest in preference domains.

Other work identifies beliefs behind aversion. Consumers resist medical AI because of "uniqueness neglect", the concern that an algorithm cannot account for a person's individual characteristics [W2942858056]. They avoid algorithmic advice partly because they assume, often wrongly, that algorithms cannot learn from mistakes [W4283162852]. Dietvorst and Bharti offer a decision-theoretic account. People are less and less bothered by each additional unit of forecasting error, so in uncertain domains they prefer higher-variance methods such as human judgment, which seem more likely to give a near-perfect answer [W2974452734].

### Further evidence for appreciation, and for over-reliance

Several studies support appreciation in advice-taking paradigms. Beyond the findings of You et al. above [W4281822284], Bogert, Schecter and Watson found people relied more on algorithmic advice than on a crowd of peers as tasks got harder, although they still penalized inaccurate advice more when it was labelled algorithmic [W3152500611]. Consumers who believe AI is smarter than humans are more likely to take algorithmic advice, but only when they see the task as complex [W3193926864].

Appreciation can also go too far. Banker and Khetani showed that consumers accepted inferior algorithmic recommendations because they believed algorithms had greater domain expertise [W4248125493]. Chong et al. found that people's self-confidence, more than their confidence in the AI, drove whether they accepted its suggestions, and that people sometimes blamed themselves and kept relying on a poorly performing AI [W3199747482]. These results support the human-factors view that the target is appropriate reliance, matched to how well the system actually performs, not reliance as such [W4243342770].

### What moderates reliance

Reviews of this literature group the causes of aversion and appreciation into several themes [W2981686111; W3024435124; W4200546216]. We focus on the four most relevant to our design.

**Task objectivity and subjectivity.** The most consistent moderator is whether a task seems to call for measurable accuracy or for human sensibility, an idea that goes back to Meehl's caution that mechanical and clinical methods may suit different tasks [W2129871510]. Lee found that for managerial decisions requiring "mechanical" skills, algorithmic and human decisions were seen as equally fair and trustworthy. For decisions requiring "human" skills, algorithmic decisions were judged less fair and trustworthy, because algorithms were seen as lacking intuition and subjective judgment [W2792183666]. Jin and Li found that people trusted algorithms more than humans in less unstructured tasks, explained by perceived accuracy, and trusted humans more in highly unstructured tasks, explained by perceived flexibility [W4415545653]. Algorithmic work is seen as less authentic than human work in a moral (sincerity) sense, though not in terms of accuracy [W2754764889]. People object to machines making moral decisions, partly because machines are seen as unable to fully think or feel [W2886363025], and to algorithms making morally relevant tradeoffs because algorithms are assumed to maximize outcomes [W3181173654].

The taste-prediction evidence, however, does not fit a simple objective/subjective split. Algorithms objectively win at predicting jokes and films [W2913854599; W2075329139], people avoid them for jokes [W2913854599], and yet people appreciate them for song and attraction forecasts [W2800068874]. This inconsistency suggests that perceived subjectivity, not the task itself, drives the effect.

**What the algorithm is compared with.** As discussed above, appreciation weakens when the algorithm competes with one's own judgment rather than another advisor [W2800068874; W4400803056]. The status of the human comparison also matters. Hou and Jung produced both aversion and appreciation by changing only how the human and algorithmic advisors were described, with perceived expertise explaining the difference [W3206874785]. Önkal et al. found the strongest discounting of statistical advice when it appeared next to a human expert [W2158570360], and Promberger and Baron show that following an expert also lets people share responsibility for the outcome [W2070125214]. An algorithm-versus-expert choice therefore represents a demanding test for appreciation.

**Performance information and errors.** Seeing an algorithm err is the most reliable trigger of aversion [W3125633690; W2600700815; W3152500611]. Berger et al. found no difference in reliance on unfamiliar human and algorithmic advisors, but did find a difference once people had seen familiar advisors err, and showing that the algorithm could learn removed that gap [W3110817755]. Turel and Kalhan show that early reliance is shaped by implicit prejudice against AI, which fades as people receive diagnostic information about performance [W4391114267]. How performance information is presented also matters. Summary error information did not reduce appreciation, but more detailed information did [W4281822284]. Revealing how an algorithm works hurts reliance when the algorithm seems too simple, while seeming too complex has no significant effect [W3189444386].

**Control.** Letting people modify an algorithm's output, even slightly, greatly increases its use [W3121705224]. A replication partly confirmed this, raised reproducibility concerns, and found that letting users choose the training algorithm also helps [W4366547314].

### Summary and positioning

Seventy years after Meehl, the accuracy advantage of formal prediction is well established, but whether people act on it is not. Studies find aversion in some settings [W3125633690; W2913854599; W2158570360; W2070125214] and appreciation in others [W2800068874; W4281822284]. Differences in what is measured, exposure to performance, task subjectivity and the type of comparison are the leading candidates for explaining the split [W2792183666; W4400803056; W3206874785]. Yet few studies vary task subjectivity systematically within a single paradigm while holding the alternative fixed as a human expert, and the taste-prediction findings point in different directions.
